video.title: Shoulder Adduction Will Transform Your Forehand Contact

classification.reason: The coach provides specific actionable drills and cues, such as finding one's natural grip without the racket first and practicing mini tennis focusing solely on feeling shoulder adduction.

problem.title_as_question: Why is horizontal shoulder adduction the key to forehand contact, and how should it be practiced?
problem.definition: Forehand contact is fundamentally produced by horizontal shoulder adduction and internal rotation. Without mastering this feeling and matching the grip and posture to it, upstream body rotation and swing speed only cause more missed shots.

symptoms.description: Erratic contact and missing shots when trying to swing faster, generate topspin, or rotate the body aggressively.
Throwing the racket awkwardly over the head on balls that arrive too close to the body.
Inability to maintain a slightly closed string angle through the hitting zone during shoulder adduction.

causes.statement: The player's grip does not match the natural horizontal shoulder adduction motion of their body, resulting in an improper string angle at contact.
The player fails to close the pectoral-humeral angle using the chest muscles to press the hand and racket forward through the hitting zone.
The player attempts to generate pace using upstream kinetic chain movements like torso torque and leg drive while the fundamental contact mechanism is broken.
On low balls, failing to tilt the torso and lower the back knee prevents the shoulder from maintaining its horizontal adduction swing plane.

angles.summary: Forehand contact is driven anatomically by the pectoral-humeral angle closing along with internal arm rotation.
Body rotation is not strictly necessary to hit a decent forehand; adduction must come first before adding upstream rotation.
Players should memorize the feeling of the chest pushing the arm forward and adapt their stance to replicate that exact sensation on any incoming ball height.

solutions.summary: Make a comfortable adduction swing motion without holding the racket, then place the racket in the hand to find the grip that naturally produces a slightly closed string angle at contact.
solutions.external_goal: Set the racket face to a slightly closed string angle at contact without forcing the hand.

solutions.summary: Hit shots keeping the chest quiet and facing forward without body rotation, solely using shoulder adduction to press through the ball.
When the ball is low, tilt the torso, drop into an athletic stance, and get the back knee down so the shoulder can adduct naturally.
During mini tennis, focus purely on feeling the horizontal shoulder adduction and finding the contact spot out in front where it happens naturally.
solutions.external_goal: Find that spot in front of you where adduction happens naturally.
